newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian armed forces impoverished, minister says.
newsitem.headline: Russian armed forces impoverished, minister says.

text.p: The Russian military is so dispirited and impoverished that officers have been forced to sell their blood to afford basic necessities, Russia's defence minister said in an interview published on Monday.

"There have been cases when officers were forced to become donors, selling their blood for money to feed their children," Igor Rodionov told Nezavisimaya Gazeta daily newspaper. "In the centuries-old history of the Russian officer corps, they have never suffered such humiliation."

Some in the air force are bringing home food from the base cafeteria to feed their families, while others are forced to sign a "debt-book" every time they make purchases in military stores because they have no money, Rodionov said.
"People are carrying out their duties at the edge of what is humanly possible," he said. "Many military families are literally starving."
The financial problems extend even to Russia's most elite military divisions, the nuclear forces.
In a rare press conference, General Igor Sergeyev, commander of Russia's strategic nuclear forces, said his men were also suffering financially.

"We haven't paid people since September, to say nothing of October, November and December. If we do not solve this acute problem, than at some stage we may lose what was always characteristic of the nuclear armed forces: stability and high-morale," he said.
"Funds are my worst headache. I've talked to the defence minister today asking him to help us pay money due since September," he said.
Sergeyev is only one of many top officers pressing Rodionov for help, as many soldiers across all divisions have not been paid in months.
The problems are so widespread that Rodionov compared the military crisis to that of 1920s after World War One and civil war, when extended fighting left the military in tatters.

"Unfortunately, our armed forces and the defence of the country as a whole are in crisis," he said. "To a certain extent, I would compare the current situation in this area to the situation of the 1920s, after the end of the civil war."

President Boris Yeltsin appointed Rodionov in July after sacking his predecessor, Pavel Grachev. Last week, Yeltsin ordered Rodionov to leave the ranks of the military to become the first civilian defence minister since 1920s.
Much of Rodionov's working day is spent worrying about financial problems, he told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. He then recounted how he had made a wish at a good luck column in India.
"I embraced it, closed my eyes and thought of the following wish," he said. "I asked God to quickly bring the army normal financing."
Initially media-shy, the silver-haired ex-general has increasingly gone public to win support for the armed forces.
In his latest interview, the defence minister complained that the draft 1997 budget passed by the lower house of parliament on Sunday did not properly fund the military.
Rodionov also said that despite the current difficulties, the defence ministry has recently prepared a plan to reform the military, which he said would soon be up for discussion.
One of his long-term reform goals is fulfilling Yeltsin's decree ending conscription and creating an all-professional army by the year 2000.
